content: The Global Competency and Outcomes Framework for Universal Health Coverage (UHC) outlines six essential domains of health worker competencies: people-centeredness, decision-making, communication, collaboration, evidence-informed practice, and personal conduct. These competencies are highly relevant to adolescent health care and are contextualized in the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Core Competencies for Adolescent Health and Development for primary care providers. All health workers in settings frequented by adolescents, such as hospitals, primary care facilities, and pharmacies, should develop these competencies. The WHO framework identifies foundational domains for adolescent health care, including basic concepts in adolescent health and development, effective communication, situational clinical care, and adherence to laws, policies, and quality standards. Health workers must understand adolescent developmental stages and their implications for clinical practice, respect adolescents’ autonomy in decision-making, and comply with quality standards for adolescent-friendly care. The WHO emphasizes the need for competency-based education in adolescent health care, both in pre-service and in-service training, to ensure lifelong learning. However, many countries lack sustainable systems for continuous professional education. Improving the structure, content, and quality of adolescent health components in pre-service curricula is critical. Competency-based education should be mandatory in the training of key professions, such as nursing, midwifery, primary care, mental health, and sexual and reproductive health (SRH) specialists. In Mauritius, recognizing the unique needs of adolescents, the Ministry of Health and Wellness (MOHW) has extended the pediatric age range from 12 to 16 years and invested in adolescent health training for pediatricians and policymakers. A master training program was conducted in April 2023 to train resource persons in adolescent-responsive services, focusing on mental health, SRH, non-communicable disease prevention, and substance use. This initiative aims to build leadership and capacity in adolescent health and well-being. In Ethiopia, where adolescents and youth make up a significant portion of the population, the Federal Ministry of Health has prioritized adolescent health in its Health Sector Transformation Plan. A National Adolescent and Youth Health Strategy highlighted the need to strengthen pre-service training curricula for adolescent health practitioners. Needs assessments revealed a lack of competent providers as a major barrier to adolescent health service delivery. The Adolescent Health and Development Curriculum was developed to address this gap, focusing on competencies such as adolescent development, effective communication, mental health assessment, prevention of risky behaviors, and gender-transformative interventions. The curriculum development process in Ethiopia involved needs assessments, content selection, and internal and external reviews. The curriculum is now being used to define competencies for in-service training, though its formal implementation has been delayed pending the development of corresponding career paths. Efforts are underway to make the curriculum more flexible for undergraduate and postgraduate students and to support continuous professional development through modular, online, and self-directed learning mechanisms. Global initiatives stress the importance of integrating adolescent-specific considerations into clinical protocols and decision-support tools. The transition from pediatric to adult care is particularly sensitive for adolescents with chronic conditions, requiring developmentally appropriate approaches. Integrated service delivery, such as combining deworming interventions with HPV vaccination and iron supplementation, is recommended to maximize efficiency and responsiveness to adolescents’ needs. Despite these efforts, adolescent health services remain fragmented and of uneven quality in many countries. Health systems often lack competence in diagnosis, management, and continuity of care for adolescents. Addressing these gaps requires alignment with national policies for quality health services and embedding adolescent-specific aspects into these policies.
